description: Fair online profiling comparison of vLLM vs SGLang — CUDA graphs enabled for both, Proton-only (no PyTorch profiler), per-rate sessions, higher loads (4, 16, 32, inf req/s)
instructions: vLLM environment: ~/vllm/.venv (activate with `. ~/vllm/.venv/bin/activate`)
SGLang environment: ~/sglang/.venv (activate with `. ~/sglang/.venv/bin/activate`)
Model: Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B (bf16) on 1x H100 80GB
Use shadow context + tree data as primary Proton config (lowest overhead)
vLLM profiling uses --profiler-config JSON with proton backend
SGLang profiling uses python -m sglang.profiler with --proton flag
SGLang default port is 30000, vLLM default port is 8000
All v2 scripts go under scripts/profiling/comparison/
All v2 output goes under profiling_output/comparison_v2/
CRITICAL FAIRNESS: CUDA graphs ENABLED for both frameworks (real-world config)
CRITICAL FAIRNESS: Proton-ONLY profiling — no torch.profiler/PyTorch GPU profiler to avoid CUPTI contention
CRITICAL FAIRNESS: each request rate must produce a separate .hatchet file — no accumulated multi-rate sessions
CRITICAL FAIRNESS: identical workload per rate — 100 prompts, input_len=1024, output_len=256, seed=42
CRITICAL FAIRNESS: both frameworks get the same warmup (10 prompts at inf rate, not profiled) before first profiled rate
vLLM Proton with CUDA graphs: already works via early-start pattern (Proton starts before graph capture)
SGLang Proton with CUDA graphs: use SGLANG_PROTON_CUDA_GRAPH=1 env var to start persistent Proton session before graph capture
SGLang profiler client: use --no-cpu --no-gpu --proton to ensure ONLY Proton subscribes to CUPTI (no torch.profiler)
SGLang --num-steps must be high enough (~30000) to not cut off before benchmark finishes
vLLM start_profile/stop_profile may accumulate into one file — may need server restart per rate to get separate files
SGLang bench_serving uses --random-input/--random-output (no -len suffix), vLLM uses --random-input-len/--random-output-len
SGLang _ProfilerProton.stop() was patched to call finalize() for non-persistent sessions
Reuse existing analyze_kernels.py for kernel categorization
REPO_ROOT for comparison scripts is 3 levels up from SCRIPT_DIR
Make clear and simple code design for ease of understanding
Write docstring and inline comments for every method
Only write absolutely necessary code, avoid redundant code, keep codebase clean
Avoid fallbacks and try-catch — fail early to discover issues at the shallow surface
Do not include claude as co-author in commit message
Do not include US-00X in commit message, follow vLLM commit message style

userStories.title: Fair vLLM online profiling script (v2)
userStories.description: As a researcher, I want a vLLM online profiling script with CUDA graphs enabled and per-rate sessions so results reflect real-world performance and are fairly comparable to SGLang.
acceptanceCriteria: Script at scripts/profiling/comparison/vllm_online_v2.sh
Activates ~/vllm/.venv before running
Starts vLLM server WITH CUDA graphs enabled (default, no --enforce-eager)
Starts vLLM server with --profiler-config JSON (profiler=proton, shadow, tree, triton) — vLLM's early-start pattern handles Proton+CUDA graph coexistence
Sends 10 warmup prompts at inf rate before profiling (not profiled)
For each rate (4, 16, 32, inf): calls /start_profile, runs vllm bench serve with --num-prompts 100 --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 256 --seed 42 --request-rate RATE, calls /stop_profile
Each rate produces a separate .hatchet file in profiling_output/comparison_v2/vllm/online/rate_N/ (restart server per rate if needed to get separate files)
Rates configurable via --request-rates arg (default: '4 16 32 inf')
Cleans up server process on exit using trap
Validates all .hatchet files with proton-viewer
Script runs successfully and produces valid per-rate .hatchet files
userStories.notes: vLLM already handles Proton+CUDA graphs via early-start pattern (Proton starts before graph capture). /start_profile and /stop_profile may accumulate into one file — test whether restarting server per rate produces separate files. Reference scripts/profiling/comparison/vllm_online.sh for patterns.

userStories.title: Fair SGLang online profiling script (v2)
userStories.description: As a researcher, I want an SGLang online profiling script with CUDA graphs enabled and Proton-only profiling so results reflect real-world performance.
acceptanceCriteria: Script at scripts/profiling/comparison/sglang_online_v2.sh
Activates ~/sglang/.venv before running
Starts SGLang server WITH CUDA graphs enabled (no --disable-cuda-graph)
Sets SGLANG_PROTON_CUDA_GRAPH=1 env var so SGLang creates persistent Proton session before CUDA graph capture (avoids CUPTI error 39)
Sends 10 warmup prompts at inf rate before profiling (not profiled)

For each rate (4, 16, 32, inf): runs sglang.profiler with --no-cpu --no-gpu --proton --proton-context shadow --proton-data tree --proton-hook triton and --num-steps 30000, concurrently runs sglang.bench_serving with --num-prompts 100 --random-input 1024 --random-output 256 --seed 42 --request-rate RATE
Each rate produces a separate .hatchet file in profiling_output/comparison_v2/sglang/online/rate_N/
Rates configurable via --request-rates arg (default: '4 16 32 inf')
Cleans up server process on exit using trap
Validates all .hatchet files with proton-viewer
Script runs successfully and produces valid per-rate .hatchet files
userStories.notes: SGLANG_PROTON_CUDA_GRAPH=1 creates persistent Proton session before graph capture. --no-cpu --no-gpu ensures ONLY Proton subscribes to CUPTI (no torch.profiler). SGLang bench_serving uses --random-input/--random-output (no -len suffix). Use --num-steps 30000 to avoid early cutoff. Reference scripts/profiling/comparison/sglang_online.sh for patterns.

Runs proton-viewer on all per-rate .hatchet files from both frameworks
Reuses kernel categorization logic from analyze_kernels.py
Produces per-rate comparison table: vLLM vs SGLang kernel category times at rates 4, 16, 32, inf
Shows how category proportions change as load increases (scaling trend)
Saves raw proton-viewer output to profiling_output/comparison_v2/analysis/
Report at profiling_output/comparison_v2/report.md
Report Section 1 — Executive Summary: key findings

Report Section 4 — Scaling Analysis: how kernel time changes from 4 to inf req/s for each framework
